preparer: Claude (Anthropic), Claude Code session; retrieval, passage finding and classification in one session against an offline cache

relations.articulates: a passage meets the proposition's criterion (schema: articulates_proposition)
relations.contests: a passage disputes the proposition or a premise it depends on (schema: contests_proposition); engagement is required
relations.bears-on: a passage bears on the proposition without meeting the criterion; the missing element is named (schema: bears_on_proposition)

engagement.engages-premise: the passage, with the turn, section or message it belongs to, gives a reason against a premise of the proposition
engagement.contrary-only: the passage states the contrary conclusion without giving a reason against such a premise

roles.earliest-located: earliest articulating or contesting tier-1 text found within the stated search scope, decided by the attested date of the checked wording; never a claim of first use
roles.earliest-located-tier-2: the same role computed separately among tier-2 texts; shown apart from the tier-1 role and never instead of it

voices.author: the author's own assertion; for co-authored texts, the text of all authors
voices.dialogue-turn: a turn by the named speaker in a multi-party dialogue

dateRule: Each source has a date (the work's own date), an attested date (the earliest retrieved copy of the checked wording) and, where given, a claimed date. Earliest located is decided by the attested date of the wording actually checked, never by a journal or later version's year; working-paper, journal and other version dates are recorded in versions. An undated file with a dated capture is dated by the capture (attested); the author's claimed date is kept separately (maintainer decision 2026-10-09).
searchScope: See scope.md: twelve texts (thirteen authored records), 1994–2024, retrieved from Wayback Machine captures on 2026-10-08.
limits: Passages relate a proposition to documented text; they do not establish that an argument or model is correct.
A model-derived passage holds only under its recorded conditions.
Figures, including G09 estimates, are each author's estimate under that author's definitions; they are not comparable without those definitions.
Quotations: at most 50 words each, at most 400 words per source, about 10% for sources under 2,000 words.

propositions.label: Machine substitution for labour produces explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that if machines (AI systems or emulated minds) can substitute for human labour across all or nearly all tasks, so that labour can be produced like capital, the growth rate of output rises far above historical rates (by roughly an order of magnitude or more) or keeps rising. The conditions under which the text derives this are part of the record.
propositions.searchNote: All twelve texts were searched for the proposition and for answers to it. Nordhaus (2015) derives the mechanism in order to test it; his test results are recorded under G06.

passages.locator: Section 7 "Discussion", paragraph beginning "These models also suggest"
passages.quote: These models also suggest that wholesale use of machine intelligence could increase economic growth rates by an order of magnitude or more.
passages.context: Summarises the paper's exogenous-growth models: once machines substitute for human labour, the labour force can be produced like capital and growth rates rise. The paper's numerical example gives 4.3% growth before and 45% after.
passages.conditions: Exogenous technology growth; computer prices halving every two years; machine labour instantly producible; diminishing returns to all inputs together; product shares chosen as "conservative" (labour 0.25, capital 0.5, computers 0.02).
passages.qualification: The author presents these as conservative estimates from deliberately simple models. Earliest located is decided by the 2000 capture of an undated file; the author dates the paper 1998 in a later citation, and that wording was not retrieved.

passages.locator: Section 7 "Discussion", same paragraph, next sentence
passages.quote: These increased growth rates are due to our assumptions that computer technology improves faster than general technology, and that the labor population of machine intelligences could grow as fast as desired to meet labor demand.
passages.context: States the two assumptions the result depends on.
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G01-a.

passages.locator: Section VII "Supply-side Singularity", paragraph beginning "The natural produced input to consider"
passages.quote: If the elasticity of substitution is greater than one, then information capital takes an increasing share of inputs, and the growth of productivity rises.
passages.context: States the model condition for a supply-side "Singularity": substitution of information capital for labour above unit elasticity. The paper then tests for the signs this mechanism would leave.
passages.conditions: Two-input production with information capital and labour; constant elasticity of substitution above one; information capital improving rapidly.
passages.qualification: Nordhaus derives the mechanism in order to test it; he does not endorse it, and his tests (G06) conclude that "the Singularity is not near". Same wording in the NBER version.

passages.locator: Section 4.1 "Examples of Technological Singularities", Example 1 "Automation of Goods Production"
passages.quote: The Type I case can emerge with full automation in the production for goods.
passages.context: With every task in goods production automated, the model becomes an AK model and ongoing productivity growth makes growth rates themselves rise over time ("Type I": growth rates rising without bound).
passages.conditions: Full automation of goods production; ongoing technological progress.
passages.qualification: One of several examples the authors construct; they also set out bottlenecks against these scenarios (G02, G04, G05).

passages.locator: Section 1 (Introduction), list of four themes, first theme "Growth theory models predict explosive growth"
passages.quote: Growth theory models often predict explosive growth by default when AI is able to substitute for human labor on most or all tasks in the economy.
passages.context: Opens the paper's summary of its assessment: substitution of AI for labour on most or all tasks makes explosive growth the default prediction of growth models.
passages.conditions: AI able to substitute for human labour on most or all tasks.
passages.qualification: Absent from v3 (2024-07-15), which rewrites the introduction; this wording is attested from v2 only.

passages.locator: Tamay Besiroglu's first long turn, paragraph beginning "Our second theme centers on"
passages.quote: I am inclined to believe that such explosive growth is not just a possibility, but a probable outcome when we transition to an era where AI automates the vast majority of tasks currently performed by humans. To put this in numbers, I'd currently assign a 65% chance
passages.context: Besiroglu defines explosive growth as at least ten times the past century's annual growth rate, sustained for at least a decade, and gives a conditional probability.
passages.speaker: Tamay Besiroglu
passages.conditions: Conditional on AI automating the vast majority of tasks; explosive growth defined as at least tenfold the past century's growth rate for a decade or more.
passages.qualification: A turn in a two-person dialogue; Matt Clancy disagrees in the next turn. At the close Besiroglu gives 25–75% "conditional on AGI".

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's closing turn, paragraph beginning "One final meta point"
passages.quote: I am nervous about relying heavily on economic models to project a break with historical experience, as I don't think the models are up to the job of making strong quantitative forecasts outside the range of historical experience.
passages.context: Clancy questions whether growth models can be extrapolated to growth far outside historical experience. Earlier in the debate he puts the chance of explosive growth at 10–20%.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.engagementRationale: Gives a reason against the premise that growth models remain reliable when extrapolated far beyond historical growth rates.
passages.qualification: Clancy does not rule explosive growth out ("I don't think explosive growth is simply impossible"); he contests the confidence placed in the model-based argument.

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's first turn, beginning "That's right"
passages.quote: I think it's maybe a 10% to 20% chance, depending on how I'm feeling, that economic growth becomes explosive, by your definition
passages.context: Clancy's answer to Besiroglu's 65%, given on the same condition of AI deployed throughout the economy. He adds that most of the probability is "clustered around the low end of explosive growth", and the same turn doubts that growth models can be extrapolated so far.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.engagementRationale: The turn gives a reason (the reach of growth models beyond historical experience) against the premise of the model-based argument.

contextOnly.reason: Shown alone, the figure could be read as Clancy endorsing explosive growth; it is his lower estimate in a disagreement.
contextOnly.requires: Besiroglu's 65% estimate and Clancy's "That's right" in reply to "I think you disagree with this view".

passages.qualification: Second passage of the same contesting record as G01-f. Moved from G09 in the correction pass (audit C05): the estimate is conditional on AI deployment, like Besiroglu's.

passages.locator: Hanson's comment, paragraph beginning "First, let me say what I agree with"
passages.quote: I can also see spurts of economic growth from plucking the "low-hanging fruit" of easy upload modifications, and due to eliminating today's biological bounds on reproduction rates of "human" type capital.
passages.context: In a comment that is otherwise sceptical of Vinge's singularity, Hanson accepts that uploads could bring bursts of growth by removing biological limits on reproducing "human" capital.
passages.missing: Describes temporary spurts of growth, not a sustained rise in the growth rate by an order of magnitude.

passages.locator: Section "A Population Explosion?", first paragraph
passages.quote: the upload population could grow at a rate far exceeding the rate at which their total wealth grows, triggering a rapid reduction in per-capita (meaning per-copy) wealth.
passages.context: If copying uploads is fast and cheap, their population could outgrow total wealth, lowering per-copy wealth.
passages.missing: States that the population of uploads grows faster than wealth; does not state that the growth rate of total output rises.
passages.qualification: Conditional on copying being "fast, cheap, and painless" and on enough uploads wanting, affording and being allowed to copy.

propositions.label: Automated research produces accelerating growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that if machines substitute for, or improve, the producers of ideas (researchers, inventors, engineers), feedback from output to research effort makes growth accelerate: super-exponential growth, growth rates rising without bound, or a finite-time singularity. The conditions under which the text derives this are part of the record.
propositions.searchNote: Texts were searched for idea-production and self-improvement feedback. A model in which technology improves with production experience (Hanson 1998) is recorded as bearing on the proposition, not as articulating it.

passages.locator: Section 4.1, Example 2 "Automation of Ideas Production", first paragraph
passages.quote: if the automation applies to the idea production function instead of (or in addition to) the goods production function. In fact, one can show that there is a mathematical singularity: a Type II event where incomes essentially become infinite in a finite amount of time.
passages.context: If an AI replaces all people in producing ideas and ideas build on earlier ideas, the model reaches infinite income in finite time.
passages.conditions: All tasks in idea production automated; returns to existing knowledge in idea production (φ) above zero.
passages.qualification: A model result. The same paper sets out "search limits" against it (G02-b).

passages.locator: Section 4.2 "Objections to singularities", subsection "Search Limits"
passages.quote: A second kind of bottleneck may occur even with complete automation. This type of bottleneck occurs when the creative search process itself prevents especially rapid producitivy gains.
passages.context: If ideas become harder to find fast enough, even fully automated research does not produce a singularity.
passages.engagementRationale: Targets the premise that automated idea production keeps sufficient returns; with strongly diminishing returns to search, growth need not explode.
passages.qualification: The same text articulates the proposition under other parameter values (G02-a); both records are needed to show its conditions. "producitivy" is the paper's spelling.

passages.locator: Hanson's comment, paragraphs beginning "Now let me be more critical" and "Can we interpret Vinge's claim"
passages.quote: If early work focuses on the easiest improvements, however, the task of becoming more productive can get harder as the easy wins are exhausted.
passages.context: Answers the claim that smarter entities produce even smarter entities faster: improvement gets harder as easy gains are used up, as with schooling, factory learning and the Flynn effect.
passages.engagementRationale: Rejects the premise that the task of self-improvement stays equally hard as intelligence rises.
passages.qualification: Written about Vinge's intelligence-explosion claim, which Hanson reads as also a claim about accelerating economic growth.

passages.locator: Hanson's comment, paragraph beginning "Can we interpret Vinge's claim as describing accelerating economic growth?"
passages.quote: A one-time reduction in the time to complete various calculations, either due to being smarter or having a faster clock, is a one-time reduction in the cost of certain types of production, which induces a one-time jump in world product.
passages.context: Argues that greater intelligence or speed changes the level of world product once, not its later growth rate. The next sentences grant that growth may rise with the size of the economy, as it has for millennia.
passages.engagementRationale: Rejects the premise that higher intelligence or speed raises the growth rate rather than the level of output.

contextOnly.reason: Alone, it reads as a denial of any growth effect; the comment immediately grants a scale effect on growth rates.
contextOnly.requires: The following two sentences on growth rates rising with the size of the world economy (G03-b).

passages.qualification: Second passage of the same contesting record as G02-c.

passages.locator: Summary, first argument ("Idea-based models of very long-run growth imply AI could drive explosive growth")
passages.quote: Suppose we develop AI systems that can substitute very effectively for human labor in producing output and in R&D. The following ideas feedback loop could occur: more ideas → more output → more AI systems → more ideas…
passages.context: Restates the ideas feedback loop of semi-endogenous growth models with AI systems in place of population, after the demographic transition broke the human loop.
passages.conditions: AI substituting very effectively for human labour in both production and R&D.
passages.qualification: Davidson's overall conclusion is probabilistic (G09-d).

passages.locator: Summary, first argument, paragraph after the feedback loop
passages.quote: Before 1880, the ideas feedback loop led to super-exponential growth. So our default expectation should be that this new ideas feedback loop will again lead to super-exponential growth.
passages.context: Draws the conclusion of the feedback argument (audit A: the first passage alone stops before it).
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G02-e.

passages.locator: Tamay Besiroglu's turn beginning "Our best models of economic growth seem to support", final paragraph
passages.quote: But with AI, our population of workers and idea producers could once again grow exponentially. What I take to be our most compelling theory of economic growth — semi-endogenous growth — implies that this will return us to what we might consider the historical trend of accelerating growth.
passages.context: Besiroglu argues that AI restores the population-ideas feedback that drove historical acceleration.
passages.speaker: Tamay Besiroglu
passages.conditions: AI that substitutes for human workers and idea producers; a semi-endogenous growth model in which ideas are non-rival and output, population and ideas feed back on each other.

passages.locator: Section 4 "Some Variations", learning-by-doing paragraph
passages.quote: Otherwise, we no longer have diminishing returns and steady growth solutions are no longer possible; our model predicts a continually accelerating growth rate.
passages.context: In a variant where technology improves with production experience, some parameter values remove diminishing returns and growth keeps accelerating. The author sets this aside to stay "conservative".
passages.missing: The feedback runs through learning by doing in production, not through machines doing research.

contextOnly.reason: Alone, it reads as the paper's headline prediction; the author presents it as a variant he does not adopt.
contextOnly.requires: The paper's statement that it sticks with exogenous growth models "to remain conservative".

passages.locator: Section 2.4 "Endogenous growth", paragraph beginning "The potential for endogenous growth processes"
passages.quote: However, since the researcher population growth rate has long been positive and the productivity growth rate has long been roughly constant, and in fact declining over recent decades (Gordon, 2016), we can infer that at least historically φ < 1.
passages.context: Infers from historical data that returns to existing knowledge in research have been below the threshold at which a constant research effort produces a finite-time singularity.
passages.missing: Concerns the historical value of a parameter; it does not say whether AI researchers, whose number can grow, would produce accelerating growth.
passages.qualification: The next sentence of the checked 2021 text gives the Bloom et al. (2020) estimate "ϕ = −2.1" (per the cross-family check; the 2023 GPI revision has the same sentence). The NBER version (2023) reads "technology growth rate" where this text has "productivity growth rate" and rounds the estimate to about −2. Corrected after the cross-family check: the earlier qualification said the NBER version added the estimate.

propositions.label: Long-run history suggests a further acceleration
propositions.criterion: The text infers from the long-run history of world output or population (hyperbolic or super-exponential growth, or a sequence of ever faster growth modes) that a future transition to much faster growth is plausible or expected.
propositions.searchNote: Kremer (1993) and von Foerster et al. (1960) are cited by several texts but were not retrieved; they are outside this scope.

passages.locator: Section 3 "The Simplest Model", paragraph after the 45% example
passages.quote: an empirical projection of historical trends in world economic growth makes a median prediction that the economy will transition to a doubling time of one to two years around 2025 (Hanson, 1998).
passages.context: Cites the author's own analysis of long-run growth (the 1998 first version of "Long-Term Growth As A Sequence of Exponential Modes") against rejecting the model's fast growth "out of hand".
passages.qualification: Added in the correction pass (audit C01). The author adds: "While this prediction has large uncertainties". A self-citation; the cited 1998 analysis was not retrieved.

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: Each mode grew world product by a factor of a few hundred, and grew a hundred times faster than its predecessor. This weakly suggests that within the next century a new mode might appear with a doubling time measured in days, not years.
passages.context: Fits world product over two million years with a few exponential "modes" (hunting, farming, industry) and extrapolates the pattern of transitions.
passages.conditions: The sum-of-exponentials or CES-combined model of growth modes; parameters of a new transition similar to those of past transitions.
passages.qualification: The author marks the inference as weak. The title page claims a first version of September 1998, which was not retrieved.

passages.locator: Hanson's comment, paragraph beginning "Can we interpret Vinge's claim"
passages.quote: this process would have been going on for millennia, and so does not suggest growth any faster than the accelerating historical "normal progress" trends suggest.
passages.context: Grants that growth rates may rise with the size of the world economy, but treats that as the long-standing accelerating trend, not a reason to expect a sudden break.
passages.missing: Uses the accelerating historical trend to bound expectations; does not infer a transition to much faster growth.

passages.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning "Having now labored long on the task"
passages.quote: I did come to appreciate that any system whose rate of growth rises with its size is inherently unstable. The human future might be one of explosion, perhaps an economic upwelling that eclipses the industrial revolution as thoroughly as it eclipsed the agricultural revolution.
passages.context: Roodman fits a stochastic super-exponential model to gross world product since prehistory and draws out its instability.

contextOnly.reason: The next sentence gives the opposite possibility, an "implosion"; quoting only the explosion branch misstates the passage.
contextOnly.requires: The following sentence: "Or the future could be one of implosion…".

passages.qualification: Roodman also writes that he doubts he has "gained much perspicacity"; the post presents possibilities, not a forecast.

passages.locator: Comment "Some personal reactions on this piece", paragraph beginning "Like David, I wouldn't take the model"
passages.quote: I tentatively agree with what I see as the central themes: that a sufficiently broad view of history shows accelerating growth, that this dynamic is inherently unstable, and that we therefore have little reason to "rule out" explosive growth in the coming decades.
passages.context: Karnofsky, who writes that he asked Roodman to evaluate Hanson's work, states what he takes from the post; he "wouldn't take the model discussed in this piece literally".
passages.qualification: A comment by a different author on Roodman's post. The same passage is recorded under G09.

passages.locator: Summary, third argument ("An ignorance perspective assigns some probability to explosive growth")
passages.quote: But we do know that the pace of growth has increased significantly over the course of history. Absent deeper understanding of the mechanics driving growth, it would be strange to rule out growth increasing again.
passages.context: An argument from history without a specific model: growth has sped up before, so a further increase should not be ruled out.

passages.locator: Tamay Besiroglu's turn beginning "In my view, accelerating growth is probably not decoupled"
passages.quote: In this sense, economic acceleration roughly on the order we're considering for this debate is perhaps actually something of a historical norm.
passages.context: Points to faster growth after the Neolithic and Industrial Revolutions, and to double-digit catch-up growth, as precedent.
passages.speaker: Tamay Besiroglu

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's turn beginning "I'm happy to grant that we have seen accelerations"
passages.quote: I think it's notable that none of the accelerations we're talking about or the rapid rates of catch-up growth experienced in the Asian tigers are typically believed to be driven by a sudden influx of intelligence into the economy.
passages.context: Clancy questions whether past accelerations are informative about an acceleration driven by intelligence.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy

contextOnly.reason: In the same turn Clancy concedes that past acceleration is "a good reason to think there is some chance it could happen again".
contextOnly.requires: The following sentence of the turn.

passages.missing: Disputes that past accelerations are informative about an acceleration driven by intelligence; G03 does not require that mechanism, and the same turn grants that past acceleration "is a good reason to think there is some chance it could happen again".
passages.qualification: Reclassified from contests after the cross-family check (G03-g); it no longer holds the earliest-located contesting role, and G03 has no contesting record.

propositions.label: Essential unautomated tasks bottleneck growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that growth is constrained because essential tasks or inputs remain unautomated or unimproved, or are automated only slowly, so that automating many but not all tasks, or automating them gradually, does not by itself produce explosive growth (Baumol's cost disease; an elasticity of substitution below one between tasks or between information and other inputs). Reasons why automation stays incomplete or slow (technical difficulty, physical-world tasks, training data, regulation of AI training or deployment, slow adoption) belong here.
propositions.searchNote: G04/G05 boundary (criterion settled 2026-10-10): a constraint is recorded under G04 when it works by keeping tasks in human hands or by slowing their automation, and under G05 when it would still bind if every task were automated. A passage is classified by the mechanism its own conclusion names; other examples in the same turn or section go in its context. Moved from G05 in this pass: G05-d → G04-k, G05-e → G04-k2 (Clancy), G05-h → G04-g2 (Erdil and Besiroglu).

passages.locator: Section IV "Singularity from the demand and the supply side", first paragraph
passages.quote: rapid growth in the productivity of computers or information technology such as shown in Figure 1 has no necessary implication for aggregate economic growth. The reason is that the economy does not run on bits alone, either on the demand side or the supply side.
passages.context: Rapid improvement in information technology raises aggregate growth only if information substitutes well for other inputs in production, or for other goods in consumption.
passages.conditions: Elasticity of substitution between information and other inputs or goods below one.

passages.locator: Section VII "Supply-side Singularity", paragraph beginning "The natural produced input to consider"
passages.quote: If the elasticity of substitution is less than one, then information capital's share in production declines over time, and the growth in aggregate productivity tends toward the growth of the relatively fixed factor, labor.
passages.context: The inelastic case of the same model: growth converges to that of the slowest input.
passages.conditions: Elasticity of substitution between information capital and labour below one.
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G04-a.

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: One theme that emerges is based on Baumol's "cost disease" insight: growth may be constrained not by what we are good at but rather by what is essential and yet hard to improve.
passages.context: The paper's organising theme, developed in its task-based models of automation.
passages.conditions: Tasks are complements (elasticity of substitution below one).

passages.locator: Section 4.1, Example 3 "Singularities without Complete Automation", first paragraph
passages.quote: With the CES case and an elasticity of substitution less than one, we require that all tasks are automated. If only a fraction of the tasks are automated, then the scarce factor (labor) will dominate, and growth rates do not explode.
passages.context: States the condition directly. The same example then shows that with Cobb-Douglas production a singularity can occur without full automation.
passages.conditions: CES production across tasks with elasticity of substitution below one.

contextOnly.reason: The next paragraph shows the opposite result under Cobb-Douglas production; the bottleneck depends on the elasticity assumption.
contextOnly.requires: The Cobb-Douglas result of the same example.

passages.locator: Section 4 "Some Variations", paragraph on exclusively human jobs
passages.quote: Having some exclusively human jobs slows growth somewhat.
passages.context: In the paper's example, a residue of human-only jobs lengthens the economic doubling time from 18 to 27 months, against 16 years without machine intelligence: growth stays far above historical rates.
passages.engagementRationale: A model result under fixed product shares (Cobb-Douglas form); it does not argue against the premise that unautomated tasks are strong complements.
passages.conditions: Product shares fixed; human-only jobs keep a share of 0.05 of output in the example.

contextOnly.reason: Alone, "slows growth somewhat" hides that growth in the example remains explosive.
contextOnly.requires: The next sentence of the paper with the 27-month doubling time.

passages.qualification: Reclassified from bears-on in the correction pass (audits B and C06).

passages.locator: Summary, objection "Automation limits", response
passages.quote: I don't think this provides a decisive reason to rule out explosive growth. Firstly, it's possible that we will ultimately automate all essential tasks, or restructure work-flows to do without them.
passages.context: Responds to the Aghion, Jones and Jones bottleneck. Davidson accepts that it "correctly highlights that AI may lead to very widespread automation without explosive growth occurring".
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that some essential task will remain unautomated, and adds that partial automation can raise growth temporarily.

passages.locator: Section 2.3 "AI automation could have massive transitory effects", paragraph beginning "Overall, even if the other arguments"
passages.quote: there's still room for explosive growth if AI can automate e.g. 90% of tasks in the economy and it can do so in a period of less than 10 years.
passages.context: Based on a CES task model calibrated with a range of substitution parameters: fast automation of most tasks can give a large transitory boost even with bottlenecks.
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that partial automation cannot produce explosive growth, by modelling a fast transition with complementary tasks.
passages.conditions: The sentence opens "even if the other arguments fail to go through and we cannot even attain AI that perfectly substitutes for humans across all tasks". CES task model with complementary tasks; a fixed stock of inputs reallocated from automated to unautomated tasks; input to automated tasks approximated as infinite (very cheap, very large AI inputs), so finite AI input would reduce the effect; about 90% of tasks automated (f = 0.1 unautomated) within less than ten years; substitution parameter ρ = −2 between tasks, below the range of −1.2 to −0.14 the authors cite as plausible for capital and labour.
passages.qualification: The authors add that they consider this argument "on shakier ground" than their other arguments. Absent from v3 (2024-07-15) in this wording. Conditions completed and context-only flag added after the cross-family check.

contextOnly.reason: Shown alone, 90% automation could read as sufficient for explosive growth; the result depends on the modelling approximations and the speed of automation.
contextOnly.requires: The recorded conditions and the authors' remark that the argument is "on shakier ground".

passages.locator: Section 3.1 "Regulations can slow down the economic impact of AI", paragraph beginning "In light of the above discussion"
passages.quote: we think our baseline scenario here for AI regulation should be more like nuclear arms control and less like the regulation of nuclear energy
passages.context: Section 3.1 treats the objection that "the training or deployment of AI systems will be sufficiently impeded by regulation"; the authors argue that incentives for AI adoption resemble those for nuclear proliferation, so coordination to slow it is likely to be imperfect.
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that regulation of AI training or deployment will keep tasks unautomated for long enough to hold growth down.
passages.qualification: Moved from G05 (formerly G05-h) under the G04/G05 criterion of 2026-10-10: the regulation discussed acts on AI training and deployment, that is, on automation. Second passage of the same contesting record as G04-g.

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's turn beginning "I think that's a fair representation", paragraph beginning "In this kind of model, what can deliver explosive growth?"
passages.quote: Either you greatly speed up the pace of automation, so that you can shift a lot more than 1% of the workforce onto the remaining tasks, or you automate 100% of the tasks necessary for innovation.
passages.context: Clancy gives a verbal version of the Aghion, Jones and Jones task model applied to innovation: with every task required and automation advancing about 1% a year, growth stays steady; only faster or full automation gives explosive growth.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.conditions: Every innovation task is required; innovation gets harder each year; displaced workers retrain onto the remaining tasks.
passages.qualification: Clancy attributes the model to Aghion, Jones and Jones and presents it as his view. Replaced in the correction pass (audits A and C04): the earlier quote was an intermediate step that Clancy corrects in his next paragraph.

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's turn beginning "As a quick aside"; his closing turn, first observation
passages.quote: my best guess at why we won't see changes as dramatic as you anticipate is because there are going to be a billion little bottlenecks that will persistently slow the rate at which AGI takes over tasks.
passages.context: Clancy says AI is "pretty likely to boost growth" and then lists bottlenecks that slow AGI's takeover of tasks: physical-world tasks, raw materials, training data, the time natural processes take, preferences for human performers, regulation and zero-sum competition.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.qualification: Moved from G05 (formerly G05-d) under the G04/G05 criterion of 2026-10-10: the passage's own conclusion is that the bottlenecks slow the rate at which AGI takes over tasks. Some items in his list (natural processes, preferences) could bind after full automation; he does not argue that they do. Same record as G04-h.

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's closing turn, first of "three broad observations"
passages.quote: First, I don't think each of these bottlenecks is enough, on its own, to short-circuit explosive growth. It's their accumulation.
passages.context: Clancy's closing turn: different sectors are held back by materials, time, data or regulation; sectors that automate easily become cheap and "no longer count for much of GDP".
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.qualification: Moved from G05 (formerly G05-e) with G04-k: the accumulation argument is a sectoral (Baumol) composition argument about uneven automation. Same record as G04-h.

passages.locator: Tamay Besiroglu's turn beginning "The usual way we think about economic bottlenecks"
passages.quote: The existence of some bottleneck tasks is not enough. You must show that there are many tasks that AI just cannot automate, say on the order of 25% or more.
passages.context: Besiroglu argues that with complementary tasks, scaling digital workers on automated tasks still raises output by one or two orders of magnitude unless a large share of tasks stays unautomated.
passages.speaker: Tamay Besiroglu
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that a few unautomated tasks suffice to block explosive growth.
passages.conditions: Tasks are complements; "digital workers" on automated tasks scaled up at least tenfold; automation going "from little to substantial" over decades rather than about a century; substitution of AI for human labour not unusually hard. In the same turn Besiroglu says that with 25% of tasks unautomated output could still rise by one or two orders of magnitude.

contextOnly.reason: The 25% figure is an illustrative threshold inside a timing argument, not a general condition for blocking explosive growth.
contextOnly.requires: The recorded conditions: the same turn ties the argument to automation within decades.

passages.qualification: Conditions and context-only flag added after the cross-family check.

propositions.label: Other constraints prevent explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that constraints that would still bind if machines performed all or nearly all tasks (physical laws or limits, natural resources and energy, the time that natural processes and experiments take, regulation of activities other than AI training and deployment, or demand for human-provided goods) can prevent or quickly end explosive growth.
propositions.searchNote: Statements that some limit must hold "eventually" are recorded as bearing on the proposition unless they say the limit binds before or soon after growth becomes explosive. See the G04 search note for the boundary test; three passages moved to G04 in the correction pass of 2026-10-10. Clancy's list of bottlenecks in the Asterisk debate includes constraints of the G05 kind (natural processes, preferences for human performers), but his argument applies them to the pace of automation; it is recorded under G04.

passages.locator: Section 4.2 "Objections to singularities", subsection "Baumol Tasks and Natural Laws"
passages.quote: A third kind of bottleneck may occur even with complete automation and even with a superintelligence. This type of bottleneck occurs when an essential input does not see much productivity growth.
passages.context: Gives physical limits, such as Carnot's theorem for energy conversion, as examples of essential inputs whose productivity cannot keep rising.
passages.conditions: Some essential input subject to physical limits on productivity; tasks are complements.

passages.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning "Basic physics suggests"
passages.quote: The relevant possibility is that AI induces a growth path that resembles these benchmarks for some time, until production confronts limiting factors, such as land or energy, that have never or have not recently been important constraints on growth.
passages.context: Treats growth-rate increases and singularities as benchmarks that hold "for some time" before limits such as land or energy bind.
passages.missing: Says limits end super-exponential growth eventually; does not say they prevent explosive growth or end it quickly.
passages.qualification: Absent from the NBER version (2023), whose introduction is rewritten.

passages.locator: Section X "Interpretations and Elaborations", subsection a "Violations of basic physical laws"
passages.quote: So the bottom line on resources is that at least in theory improvements in material use and miniaturization can overcome the physical limitations on accelerating growth.
passages.context: Raises the objection that energy, water, minerals and thermodynamics limit accelerating growth, and answers it with the fall in energy needed per computation since ENIAC.
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that physical resource needs bind, because inputs per unit of output can fall as fast as production rises.
passages.qualification: Added in the correction pass (audit C03). Nordhaus calls the issues "too deep to be adequately treated in the present study"; his own tests find no approach to a singularity (G06).

passages.locator: Summary, objection "Limits to how fast a human economy can grow", response
passages.quote: I do think that there is some chance that one of these bottlenecks will prevent explosive growth. On the other hand, no individual bottleneck is certain to apply and there are some reasons to think we could grow at 30% per year
passages.context: Responds to a list of bottlenecks (regulation, materials, physical experiments, human adjustment, fundamental limits) with incentives to remove them, past 10% catch-up growth and 30% growth of individual businesses.
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that any one listed bottleneck is certain to bind, while granting "some chance" that one does.

contextOnly.reason: The passage opens with a concession; quoting only the concession or only the rebuttal misstates it.

passages.qualification: Davidson's appendix puts about 25% on such a bottleneck preventing explosive growth. G04/G05 boundary (2026-10-10): kept under G05 because Davidson responds to bottlenecks offered against explosive growth from AI that substitutes for labour; the list also includes regulation and human adjustment, which may act on the pace of automation. The surrounding text could not be re-read in this pass, so this classification is uncertain.

passages.locator: Tamay Besiroglu's turn beginning "I agree that reality is messy", paragraph on resource bottlenecks
passages.quote: I remain unconvinced by the arguments of specific resource bottlenecks that people often bring up.
passages.context: Besiroglu sets three conditions a resource bottleneck must meet (vital, hard to substitute, impossible to expand by an order of magnitude); he also argues that experiments can be parallelised and that regulation faces strong incentives to be bypassed.
passages.speaker: Tamay Besiroglu
passages.engagementRationale: Gives reasons in the same turn against the premises that resource limits and experiment times bind.
passages.qualification: On regulation the same turn says only that its effect "is plausible, but I'm not confident it will" keep growth near historical rates.

passages.locator: Section 3.2 "Output is bottlenecked by other non-accumulable factors of production", paragraph containing "there might be intrinsic timescales"
passages.quote: Some version of this argument is certainly sound: there must eventually be some resource constraints that prevent output from growing arbitrarily large. The important question about this argument is not whether it holds eventually, but whether it holds quickly enough to preclude explosive growth.
passages.context: Accepts eventual limits and contests their timing, with an estimate of returns to scale.
passages.engagementRationale: Disputes the premise that resource constraints bind soon enough to preclude explosive growth.

propositions.label: Current data show no approach to explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states, on the basis of current or recent economic data, that the economy shows no sign yet of approaching a growth singularity or explosive growth.
propositions.searchNote: Only Nordhaus (2015) applies formal tests. Under the literal criterion ("no sign yet") his record bears on G06, because two of his seven tests are positive (cross-family check, 2026-10-09). Whether to reword G06 is an open decision for the maintainer; under a reworded criterion ("no persuasive evidence of a near-term approach") his record would be reassessed. No text in scope disputes his test results; Davidson (2021) disputes their bearing on horizons beyond two decades.

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: The tests suggest that the Singularity is not near.
passages.context: Six diagnostic tests on US data (productivity growth, capital share, capital prices, capital-output ratio, information capital share, wage growth) plus a demand-side test.
passages.conditions: Singularity defined in the paper as "a time when the economic growth rate crosses 20% per year"; tests on US data to about 2014.
passages.missing: Nordhaus reports two of seven tests positive for Singularity; he concludes that it is "not near", not that the data show no sign of approach. Under the literal criterion ("no sign yet") the record bears on G06.
passages.qualification: Reclassified from articulates after the cross-family check; the G06 wording question is an open decision in the project document.

passages.locator: Section IX "Summary of Tests for Singularity"
passages.quote: Five of the seven tests are negative for Singularity while two are positive.
passages.context: For the two positive tests, simple extrapolation puts the crossing point 100 years or more away.
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G06-a. Reclassified from articulates after the cross-family check; the G06 wording question is an open decision in the project document.
passages.missing: Nordhaus reports two of seven tests positive for Singularity; he concludes that it is "not near", not that the data show no sign of approach. Under the literal criterion ("no sign yet") the record bears on G06.

passages.locator: Summary, objection "There's no evidence of explosive growth in any economic sub-sector", response
passages.quote: The absence of these signs in macroeconomic data is reason to doubt explosive growth will occur within the next couple of decades. Beyond this time frame, it is hard to draw conclusions.
passages.context: Responding to the objection that macroeconomic data show none of the signs explosive growth would leave (the objection cites Nordhaus (2021)), Davidson accepts the absence of signs for the next two decades and limits its reach beyond.

contextOnly.reason: Davidson limits the inference to the next couple of decades.
contextOnly.requires: The next sentence ("Beyond this time frame, it is hard to draw conclusions") and his remark that fast growth in machine learning could be an early sign.

passages.qualification: Reclassified from bears-on after the cross-family check: G06 does not require the author to examine the data. The 2021 page could not be re-read in this pass (Wayback connection resets; the current host refuses requests); the quotation was verified on 2026-10-08 and in the cross-family check against the recorded captures.

passages.locator: Matt Clancy's turn beginning "As a quick aside"
passages.quote: note that the 100-million-fold increase in computing power dedicated to AI over the last decade has not led to an acceleration in economic growth so far.
passages.context: Clancy answers Besiroglu's point about fast growth in AI training compute.
passages.speaker: Matt Clancy
passages.qualification: An observation, not a formal test. He adds that AI is "pretty likely to boost growth".

propositions.label: Machine substitution drives wages down
propositions.criterion: The text states that once machines substitute for human labour at falling cost, the market wage of human labour falls (towards the cost of machine labour, or below subsistence), even while total output or wealth rises.
propositions.searchNote: Nordhaus (2015) states the proposition for unskilled labour only and, in his main model with imperfect substitution, has wages growing rapidly; that model result was not recorded as a contesting record. Trammell and Korinek (2020) survey the range of wage outcomes and relay Hanson's model; those passages were not recorded. Besiroglu's remark in the Asterisk debate that "human labor may lose most, if not almost all, of its value" was seen and not recorded.

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: With evolved values, most uploads would value life even when life is hard or short, uploads would reproduce quickly, and wages would fall. But total wealth should rise
passages.context: If brain emulations can be copied cheaply and selection favours those willing to work for little, copying continues until wages approach subsistence.
passages.conditions: Uploads can be copied fast and cheaply; values evolve under selection; copying is not forcibly prevented.
passages.qualification: Dated 1994 on the reprint; the earliest retrieved wording is the 1998 capture.

passages.locator: Section "The Evolution of Values", first paragraph
passages.quote: Per-capita wages seem likely to fall in this period, for ordinary humans as well as uploads, though total wealth should rise.
passages.context: Names human wages explicitly, for the period in which the upload population expands.
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G07-a (audit B).

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: At first, complementary effects dominate, and human wages rise with computer productivity. But eventually substitution can dominate, making wages fall as fast as computer prices now do.
passages.context: In the paper's model, wages first rise and later fall at the rate of computer price declines, while growth rates rise.
passages.conditions: Exogenous-growth model with machine labour substituting for human labour; falling computer prices.
passages.qualification: The paper adds that falling wages "may be consistent with a rapidly rising per-capita income for humans" if humans keep a share of capital.

passages.locator: Section 3 "The Simplest Model", paragraph after the wage equations
passages.quote: Wages might well fall below human subsistence levels, if machine subsistence levels were lower.
passages.context: States the extreme case of the model's wage path.
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G07-b.

passages.locator: Section X, subsection b "Heterogeneous labor in the growth model"
passages.quote: The marginal product and wage of unskilled labor fall proportionally with capital prices.
passages.context: A polar case of his model with heterogeneous labour; skilled labour, an imperfect substitute, fares differently.
passages.conditions: Unskilled labour a perfect substitute for information capital; skilled labour highly but imperfectly substitutable.

contextOnly.reason: Applies to unskilled labour in one polar case; in the main model wages grow rapidly.
contextOnly.requires: The case assumptions, recorded in conditions.

passages.qualification: Added in the correction pass (audit C12).

propositions.label: AI's near-term aggregate productivity effect is modest
propositions.criterion: The text estimates or states that the effect of AI on aggregate productivity or GDP over roughly the next decade will be modest: a small effect on the level of output, not a change in the growth regime.
propositions.searchNote: Only one text in scope makes a decade-scale estimate. Forecasts that Acemoglu relays (Goldman Sachs, McKinsey Global Institute, Korinek and Suh) were not retrieved.

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: these macroeconomic effects appear nontrivial but modest—no more than a 0.71% increase in total factor productivity over 10 years.
passages.context: A task-based estimate using Hulten's theorem: the share of tasks exposed to AI times the average task-level cost saving.
passages.conditions: Task-based model; cost savings at the task level; existing estimates of exposure (about 4.6% of tasks affected within ten years) and of cost savings (15.4%).

passages.locator: Section 1 (Introduction), paragraph on investment effects
passages.quote: GDP is also estimated to grow by around 1.1% over the next 10 years.
passages.context: The GDP effect after an assumed investment response; under the investment assumptions of earlier automation the upper bound rises to 1.6–1.8%.

contextOnly.reason: The figure is a cumulative level effect over ten years and can be misread as an annual growth rate.

passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G08-a. The figure is a level effect over ten years, not an annual growth rate.

propositions.label: Explosive growth estimates within a stated horizon
propositions.criterion: The text states its own estimate of whether or when explosive growth (as the text defines it) occurs in the actual future, with machine intelligence or automation among the stated drivers. Each record gives the holder, the estimate as stated (a number or words), the horizon, the text's definition and the conditions. Records are not converted to a common threshold, combined or ranked; a low estimate and a high estimate both articulate this proposition.
propositions.searchNote: Replaces the earlier criterion with a threshold of about 10% (maintainer decision 2026-10-09). Conditional estimates are recorded with their condition; the Asterisk estimates also stay under G01 as part of the mechanism debate. Acemoglu (2024) gives a ten-year estimate for current AI and no explosive-growth estimate (bears-on; see G08). Roodman (2020) reports a model projection that he does not present as a forecast; not recorded as an estimate.

passages.locator: Section 3 "The Simplest Model", paragraph after the 45% example
passages.quote: an empirical projection of historical trends in world economic growth makes a median prediction that the economy will transition to a doubling time of one to two years around 2025 (Hanson, 1998).
passages.context: The next sentence: the prediction "suggests that we not reject out of hand the predictions of this model of machine intelligence", and the following one links 2025 to brain-equivalent computer hardware.
passages.qualification: Same passage as G03-0; counted once towards the quotation limit. Added in the correction pass (audit C02). The author adds that the prediction "has large uncertainties".

estimate.value: median prediction of a transition to an economic doubling time of one to two years
estimate.horizon: around 2025 (measured from an undated file attested 2000)
estimate.definition: doubling time of world product of one to two years
estimate.conditions: "an empirical projection of historical trends in world economic growth"; the author adds that it "has large uncertainties" and links 2025 to brain-equivalent computer hardware in the next sentence.

passages.locator: Paragraph beginning "In summary, if one takes seriously" (pp. 15–16), in the section after "Interpreting the Modes"
passages.quote: it seems hard to escape the conclusion that the world economy could see a very dramatic change within the next century, to a new economic growth mode with a doubling time of roughly two weeks or less.
passages.context: The next sentences point to falling computer hardware costs, predicted machine substitution for most human labour, and his own model of growth with robots.
passages.conditions: "if one takes seriously the model of economic growth as a series of exponential growth modes, and if relative change parameters of a new transition are likely to be similar to such parameters describing old transitions".

contextOnly.reason: The sentence is the consequent of a two-part conditional; without the condition it reads as an unconditional forecast.
contextOnly.requires: The preceding conditional clause, recorded in conditions.

estimate.value: "hard to escape the conclusion that the world economy could see a very dramatic change"
estimate.definition: a new growth mode with a doubling time of roughly two weeks or less
estimate.conditions: If the series-of-modes model is taken seriously and a new transition resembles past ones.

passages.locator: Paragraph beginning "In summary, if one takes seriously" (p. 16), later sentence
passages.quote: Simple formal models have even been developed suggesting that adding robots to very standard growth models can allow growth rates to naturally increase by a factor of ten, a hundred, or even more (Hanson, 1998).
passages.context: Links the forecast to machine substitution for labour, citing his own 1998 paper (G01-a).
passages.qualification: Second passage of the same record as G09-a; a self-citation. The sentence reports a model result and is not itself a forecast.

passages.locator: Comment "Some personal reactions on this piece", paragraph beginning "Like David, I wouldn't take the model"
passages.quote: I tentatively agree with what I see as the central themes: that a sufficiently broad view of history shows accelerating growth, that this dynamic is inherently unstable, and that we therefore have little reason to "rule out" explosive growth in the coming decades.
passages.context: The same comment says he independently holds that transformative AI "could plausibly be developed in the next couple of decades".
passages.qualification: Same passage as G03-d; counted once towards the quotation limit.

estimate.conditions: Tentative agreement with Roodman's themes; the same comment says transformative AI "could plausibly be developed in the next couple of decades".

passages.locator: Abstract
passages.quote: Ultimately, I find that explosive growth by 2100 is plausible but far from certain.
passages.context: Explosive growth is defined in the report as more than 30% annual growth of gross world product.
passages.conditions: Explosive growth defined as >30% annual GWP growth; horizon 2100.

estimate.value: "plausible but far from certain"; >10% (Appendix G); "as low as 15% or as high as 60%" on different days
estimate.definition: more than 30% annual growth of gross world product
estimate.conditions: Overall judgement across the report's models and objections.

passages.locator: Appendix G "How I decide my overall probability of explosive growth by 2100"
passages.quote: What is robust is that I assign non-negligible probability (>10%) to explosive growth, exponential growth, and sub-exponential growth.
passages.context: Follows: "On a different day my probability of explosive growth by 2100 might be as low as 15% or as high as 60%."

passages.locator: Section IX "Summary of Tests for Singularity"
passages.quote: Using simple extrapolation for the two positive tests, the time at which the economy might plausibly cross the Singularity is 100 years or more.
passages.context: Extrapolating the two positive tests puts growth above 20% a year at least a century away.
passages.qualification: Reclassified from contests after the cross-family check: a horizon of 100 years or more overlaps "about a century" and gives no probability. Under the estimate criterion of 2026-10-09 it is Nordhaus's own estimate.

estimate.value: the economy "might plausibly cross the Singularity" in "100 years or more"
estimate.definition: economic growth rate crossing 20% per year
estimate.conditions: Simple extrapolation of the two of seven tests that are positive; no probability and no duration given.

tiers.1: scholarly work by economists in any venue (journal articles, working papers, books, chapters, commission reports, and essays or articles they wrote in magazines), and any text in a core economics venue (economics journals and economics working-paper series) whoever wrote it
tiers.2: texts by non-economists, whatever the venue; and short-form commentary even by economists (blog comments, forum replies, magazine or online debates), unless a turn is itself a substantive scholarly argument, which is recorded as a judgement; labelled as tier 2
tiers.rule: Maintainer decision 2026-10-11, superseding the venue-first rule of 2026-10-09. The author decides, not the venue: a scholarly text is tier 1 when an author is an economist, shown by an economics appointment, degree, address or affiliation in or near the text, or by an established record as an economist. Short-form commentary is tier 2 whoever wrote it. A core economics venue is tier 1 whoever wrote in it. Each source records its tier and a one-line basis; judgements are marked as such.

estimateFields: G09 records carry estimate: holder (the author or speaker whose estimate it is), value (the estimate as the text states it, number or words), horizon (as stated, with the year it is measured from), definition (the text's own definition of explosive or very fast growth), conditional (true when the text conditions the estimate on an assumption) and conditions. Estimates are never converted to a common threshold or combined.
